Part B · Chapter B1

One neuron

A weighted sum, then a bend. Linear regression, logistic regression and the perceptron are one neuron with different activations.

A neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds a bias and applies an activation. With no activation it has the form of the line of A2, with a sigmoid that of the logistic regression of A3, and with a step it is the perceptron. Tune a neuron on two kinds of sharks, then form a layer.

The sharks are made up: records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data.

You will need: the dot product and matrix as a layer, the sigmoid curve, the slopes of the activations, and the model chapters A2 and A3.

A neuron, taken apart

Guess first. A neuron multiplies its two inputs by weights, adds a bias to get the weighted sum \(z\), and applies an activation to \(z\). The map in the figure shows the output for all pairs of inputs. ReLU keeps positive values and turns negative ones into 0. If the activation changes from "none" to "ReLU", which part of the map changes: where \(z\) is positive, or where \(z\) is negative?

A neuron with two inputs has three parameters, numbers that fitting usually adjusts. Here \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) are weights that multiply the inputs \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), and \(b\) is the bias, a number added to their sum. The result is the weighted sum \(z\), and the activation \(g\) is a function that turns \(z\) into the output \(a\).

  1. The star is the input \((x_1, x_2)\) and the dashed line is where \(z = 0\). Choose "none" and then "ReLU": only the half of the map where \(z\) is negative changes, and it turns flat at 0.
  2. Set the weight \(w_2\) to 0: \(z\) then has no \(x_2\) in it, so the stripes (bands of equal output) turn vertical and the output ignores \(x_2\).
  3. With the sigmoid, double \(w_1\), \(w_2\) and \(b\): \(z\) is 0 at the same points, so the dashed line stays, and the stripes move closer, since \(z\) changes twice as fast.
No activationthe output is \(z\) itself: linear regression (A2)
Sigmoidthe output is a probability: logistic regression (A3)
Stepthe output is 0 or 1: the perceptron (section 3)
tanh, ReLU, GELUthe choices inside deeper networks (B2)

ReLU changes only the half where \(z\) is negative, and for all six activations the output is constant along lines parallel to the dashed line.

How it works

At the starting settings of the figure the inputs are \(x_1 = 0.8\) and \(x_2 = 0.4\), the weights are \(w_1 = 1.5\) and \(w_2 = -1.0\), and the bias is \(b = 0.3\). With these values the weighted sum is \(z = 1.5 \times 0.8 + (-1.0) \times 0.4 + 0.3 = 1.10\). The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) turns \(z\) into a number between 0 and 1: \(e^{-1.10} = 0.333\), so \(a = 1/(1 + 0.333) = 0.750\).

\(a\)output, 0.750=\(g\)activation, sigmoid(\(w_1\)weight, 1.5×\(x_1\)input, 0.8+\(w_2\)weight, −1.0×\(x_2\)input, 0.4+\(b\)bias, 0.3)=g(\(z\)weighted sum, 1.10)

The weights \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) determine how strongly the inputs move \(z\), and so the direction in which the output changes. Adding the bias \(b\) shifts \(z\), and so moves the line where \(z = 0\), the boundary of the neuron's decision. The activation \(g\) then determines how the output rises across that line: with no activation the output is \(z\) itself. A second example, Tag 4127 (the shark of the first practice exercise), repeats these steps in the fold below.

Common belief. A curved activation such as the sigmoid or tanh lets a neuron draw a curved boundary.

Why it fails. The output depends on the input only through \(z\), and all points with the same \(z\) lie on one straight line.

Better account. A neuron with an activation that never decreases (all but GELU) has one straight boundary line, and GELU, which dips below 0 first, can give two parallel lines. Curved boundaries need several neurons (the next chapter).

Quick quiz

A neuron has \(w_1 = 2\), \(w_2 = -1\), \(b = -1\) and no activation. What is its output for \(x_1 = 1\) and \(x_2 = 3\)?

\(z = 2 \times 1 + (-1) \times 3 + (-1) = -2\). With no activation the output is \(a = z = -2\).

You add 5 to the bias. Does the line \(z = 0\) move, turn, or stay?

It moves, parallel to itself. The direction depends only on \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), so the line does not turn. The bias slides it across the map.

Go deeper symbols, two more examples, Python about 9 min

Reading the figure

The weighted sum \(z\) is the same \(z\) that logistic regression uses. The star on the map is the input \((x_1, x_2)\). Two sliders move it, and so does a click or a drag on the map. The three dials \(w_1\), \(w_2\) and \(b\) set the weighted sum. The dashed line is where \(z = 0\). The coral arrow \(\mathbf{w}\) points in the direction in which \(z\) rises fastest, and it always meets the dashed line at a right angle. The curve on the left is the activation, with a teal dot at the current \(z\). The boxes above the curve show the arithmetic with the numbers you chose. With no activation the output is \(z\) itself, and with the sigmoid it is a number between 0 and 1. The activation changes only how the output rises across the line \(z = 0\), not where the line is. With ReLU the half where \(z\) is positive looks the same as with no activation. Doubling the three dials makes the output switch from near 0 to near 1 over a shorter distance.

Why the stripes are straight

The straight stripes have a reason. The output depends on the input only through \(z\), and \(z\) is constant along any line \(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 = \text{const}\). So a single level of the output, such as \(a = 0.5\) for the sigmoid, is a straight line. That is the decision boundary of A3, and it is why one neuron with an activation that never decreases can only cut the plane with one line. GELU dips below 0 before it rises, so a threshold on its output can give two parallel lines.

Checking the right angle with numbers

The right angle between the arrow and the dashed line is easy to check with numbers. Take the starting dials \(\mathbf{w} = (1.5, -1.0)\) and \(b = 0.3\). The points \((0, 0.3)\) and \((1, 1.8)\) both lie on the line. The first has \(z = 1.5 \times 0 - 1.0 \times 0.3 + 0.3 = 0\). The second has \(z = 1.5 \times 1 - 1.0 \times 1.8 + 0.3 = 0\). The step between them is \((1, 1.5)\), and its dot product with \(\mathbf{w}\) is \(1.5 \times 1 + (-1.0) \times 1.5 = 0\). A step along the line has no component along \(\mathbf{w}\), which is what a right angle means (0.5). The distance from the origin to the line is \(|b| / \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 0.3 / 1.80 = 0.17\). So the bias alone does not fix where the line is: a larger weight vector brings the line closer to the origin for the same bias.

Symbols

\[ z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b \qquad\qquad a = g(z) \]

  • \(x_1, x_2\) are the inputs, collected in the vector \(\mathbf{x}\). \(w_1, w_2\) are the weights, collected in \(\mathbf{w}\). The product \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}\) is the dot product of 0.5.
  • \(b\) is the bias. With \(b = 0\) the line \(z = 0\) must pass through the point where both inputs are 0, which is a strong restriction.
  • \(g\) is the activation and \(a\) is the output. With \(d\) inputs the sum has \(d\) weights and one bias, so \(d + 1\) numbers in all, and the boundary is a flat plane with \(d - 1\) dimensions.

The same neuron in Python: Tag 3305

import numpy as np

x = np.array([41.0, 11.5])                      # Tag 3305: length and girth, cm
mean, spread = np.array([39.138, 10.993]), np.array([8.614, 2.455])
w, b = np.array([4.732, -0.1215]), 2.4811       # the weights fitted in A3

xs = (x - mean) / spread                        # scale the inputs, as in A2
z = w @ xs + b                                  # 1. weighted sum
a = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))                        # 2. activation (sigmoid)
print(f"z = {z:.2f}, output a = {a:.3f}")       # 3. the neuron's output
z = 3.48, output a = 0.970

Three lines are the neuron. The numbers are the logistic regression of A3: the same weights give the same weighted sum of 3.48 (the score of A3) and the same probability of 0.970 for Tag 3305. A logistic regression is a one-neuron network.

A second worked example: Tag 4127

Here is the same neuron on a second shark, one step at a time. Tag 4127 is the juvenile bamboo shark from the Juhu rock pool: 44.0 cm long, with a girth of 12.4 cm. Step 1 scales both inputs, as in A2. Step 2 forms the weighted sum. Step 3 applies the sigmoid.

0.564scaled length=(44.0length, cm−39.138mean length)÷8.614spread
0.573scaled girth=(12.4girth, cm−10.993mean girth)÷2.455spread
5.08weighted sum z=4.732weight on length×0.564scaled length+−0.1215weight on girth×0.573scaled girth+2.481bias
0.994output a=σ(5.08weighted sum z)

The products are 2.671 and \(-0.070\), and the sum with the bias is 5.082. The output 0.994 is read as a probability of 99.4% that the shark is an adult, and that is wrong: Tag 4127 is a juvenile. The weights were fitted to spadenose sharks, which mature at about 35 cm, while bamboo sharks mature at about 53 cm. A neuron fitted to one kind of shark can still give a value near 0 or 1 for another kind. A high output therefore does not show that the call is right (A3). The first practice exercise uses this neuron, whose weights were fitted in A3 on the length and girth of spadenose sharks.

Another reading: the weights as votes

Another way to read the neuron: the weights are votes, and the bias sets how many votes it takes to say yes. For Tag 4127 the length votes \(+2.671\), the girth votes \(-0.070\), and the bias adds \(+2.481\), so the sum comes almost entirely from the length vote and the bias, and the girth vote is close to 0. The picture breaks when the inputs interact. A neuron adds its votes and never multiplies them. It can give length one vote and depth another, but the vote of length cannot change with the depth. Cases of that kind need more than one neuron (B2).

A third example: Woman A

A third neuron reads the clinic's Pima rows. This is a published dataset of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, and not data from Mumbai. Woman A has a glucose of 158 mg/dL and a BMI of 31.6. The 614 training women have a mean glucose of 120.9 with a spread of 32.0, and a mean BMI of 32.0 with a spread of 7.7. So her scaled inputs are \((158 - 120.9)/32.0 = 1.16\) and \((31.6 - 32.0)/7.7 = -0.05\). Take the dials of the unit in my project primer, with a ReLU activation:

0.70output a=ReLU(1.5weight on glucose×1.16scaled glucose+0.8weight on BMI×−0.05scaled BMI+−1.0bias)

The sum inside is \(1.74 - 0.04 - 1.00 = 0.70\). It is positive, so ReLU passes it on unchanged. Now swap in the dials that training finds for a sigmoid neuron on the 614 women: weights 1.11 and 0.65, bias \(-0.83\). The sum is \(z = 1.287 - 0.032 - 0.83 = 0.425\) and \(\sigma(0.425) = 0.605\). Her glucose, 1.16 spreads above the mean, drives the sum. Her BMI is close to the mean and hardly moves it. This neuron gives Woman A a probability of about 60% for diabetes, and she did have diabetes. Over the 614 women it was fitted on, it calls 468 right (76.2%), against 65.3% for always saying "no". The same inputs with another activation give another kind of number: 0.70 is a plain number (ReLU does not limit it to between 0 and 1), and 0.605 is a probability.

import numpy as np

# Woman A: glucose 158 mg/dL, BMI 31.6 (a published Pima row, not Mumbai data)
x = np.array([158.0, 31.6])
# mean and spread of glucose and BMI over the 614 training women
mean, spread = np.array([120.855, 31.983]), np.array([32.035, 7.741])
xs = (x - mean) / spread  # scale, as in A2
print("scaled inputs:", np.round(xs, 3))

z = np.array([1.5, 0.8]) @ xs - 1.0  # the ReLU dials
print(f"ReLU dials:    z = {z:.3f}, output = {max(0.0, z):.3f}")
z = np.array([1.11, 0.65]) @ xs - 0.83  # dials found for a sigmoid
print(f"sigmoid dials: z = {z:.3f}, output = {1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)):.3f}")
scaled inputs: [ 1.16  -0.049]
ReLU dials:    z = 0.700, output = 0.700
sigmoid dials: z = 0.425, output = 0.605

Why it is called a neuron

The name comes from nerve cells, which collect signals from many other cells and pass on a signal that is stronger when the total is larger. The artificial neuron is a formula. It has no timing, no chemistry and no living cell. Most activations give a smooth number and do not fire or stay quiet. The name stays because the picture of inputs, weights and one output is useful.

In practice

In practice: inputs are usually scaled to a mean of 0 and a spread of 1. Weights usually start small and random, with a size that depends on the number of inputs (often 0.1 to 1 when there are only a few). The bias usually starts at 0. A weight means something only next to the scale of its input: 0.5 per centimetre is a large weight, and 0.5 per spread is a small one. Compare the size of two weights only after scaling. In the neuron for Tag 4127 the weights are 4.732 on length and \(-0.1215\) on girth, so per spread of the input the weight on length is about 39 times the weight on girth.

Used in: a network is many such neurons wired in rows (section 4) and in stacks (B2). My diabetes screening app runs a small neural network, and my project primer has a one-unit figure on glucose and BMI.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a sigmoid neuron outputs 0 or 1 for all inputs, print \(z\). A large \(|z|\) means the sigmoid is saturated, and the usual cause is inputs on a large scale, such as lengths in centimetres next to depths in metres. Scale the inputs first (A2). Suppose Tag 4127's length and girth go in unscaled. Then \(z = 4.732 \times 44.0 - 0.1215 \times 12.4 + 2.481 = 209.2\). The sigmoid gives 1.000 for this shark and for all the others.

More questions

In the ReLU neuron for Woman A, the weight on glucose changes from 1.5 to \(-1.5\) and the other dials stay as they were. What is her output?

\(z = -1.5 \times 1.16 + 0.8 \times (-0.05) - 1.0 = -1.74 - 0.04 - 1.00 = -2.78\). ReLU turns a negative sum into 0, so the neuron is switched off for her.

Six activations

Guess first. A sigmoid neuron has a weighted sum of \(z = 8\), so its output is 0.9997. You raise \(z\) by 1. Does the output change by a large amount or by a small amount? And what about a ReLU neuron at \(z = 8\)?

The six activations are: none, \(g(z) = z\); the step, 1 if \(z \ge 0\) and 0 otherwise; the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\); and tanh, a curve like the sigmoid that runs from \(-1\) to 1. The other two are ReLU, \(\max(0, z)\), and GELU, \(z\,\Phi(z)\), a smooth version of ReLU in which \(\Phi(z)\) is the share of a standard normal distribution below \(z\). They differ in where they are flat and where they have slope \(g'(z)\), the change in the output for a small change in \(z\). A neuron on a flat tail of the curve, where the slope is close to 0, is saturated: a change in its weights hardly changes its output.

  1. With the sigmoid chosen, drag \(z\) from end to end. The navy curve is the output, the dashed sand curve is its slope, and the slope drops towards 0 in both tails.
  2. Drag \(z\) to the right end, 6, and compare the sigmoid with ReLU: the sigmoid's slope is about 0.0025 (the figure shows 0.002), while ReLU's is still 1.

The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, about 0.0025 at \(z = 6\) and 0.0003 at \(z = 8\), while ReLU's slope is still 1.

How it works

At \(z = 2\) the sigmoid gives \(\sigma(2) = 1/(1 + e^{-2}) = 1/(1 + 0.135) = 0.881\), so its slope is \(0.881 \times 0.119 = 0.105\). ReLU has slope 1 for positive \(z\) and 0 for negative \(z\). A ReLU neuron whose \(z\) is negative for all inputs is a dead unit: its slope is 0, so gradient descent changes none of its weights.

\(\sigma'(z)\)slope, 0.105=\(\sigma(z)\)output, 0.881×\(1-\sigma(z)\)distance from 1, 0.119

The sigmoid's slope is the product of its output and the distance of that output from 1, so it is largest, 0.25, at \(z = 0\), where both are 0.5. The slope of the tanh also peaks at \(z = 0\), at 1. In the tails one factor is close to 0, so the slope falls below 0.01 when \(|z|\) exceeds 4.6. Gradient descent, the usual fitting method, changes a weight in small steps (updates) that usually contain the slope as a factor. At \(z = 8\) the slope is 0.000335, about 750 times smaller than 0.25, so the same change in the weights takes about 750 times as many steps if the other factors are equal. Section 3 shows an exception: a sigmoid output trained with log loss.

Common belief. ReLU is two straight pieces, so it is no different from using no activation.

Why it fails. For one neuron the difference is small, because the boundary stays a straight line. In a stack the corner of ReLU at 0 matters, because without a corner the layers collapse to one layer (the next chapter).

Better account. The activation also decides which slopes stay large when many layers multiply them (backpropagation and deep networks).

Quick quiz

At \(z = 0\), which has the larger slope: the sigmoid or tanh?

The tanh: its slope is 1 at \(z = 0\), against 0.25 for the sigmoid.

A ReLU neuron has \(z = -3\) for the shark you are looking at. What happens to the weights if you train on that shark alone?

The weights do not change. The slope is 0, so this shark gives the update no slope to follow.

Go deeper slopes, GELU, table, derivations, Python about 7 min

Reading the figure

Choose "All six side by side" to compare where the curves are steep and where they are flat. The slider for \(z\) ends at 6, so the values at \(z = 8\) in the text come from the formulas. The slope peaks at \(z = 0\) for the sigmoid and drops close to 0 in both tails.

Slopes at z = 2, worked

The tanh gives \(\tanh 2 = 0.964\), so its slope is \(1 - 0.964^2 = 0.071\). For GELU, \(\Phi(2) = 0.9772\) and \(\varphi(2) = 0.0540\), so the slope is \(0.9772 + 2 \times 0.0540 = 1.085\). ReLU has a slope of 1. At \(z = 2\) a small nudge to \(z\) therefore moves a sigmoid output by 10.5% of the nudge, a tanh output by 7.1% and a ReLU output by all of it. Tanh starts steeper than the sigmoid (1 against 0.25 at \(z = 0\)) and falls faster, so it saturates sooner. The 750 in the text above is the same arithmetic at \(z = 8\). There \(\sigma(8) = 0.999665\), so \(1 - \sigma(8) = 0.000335\). The slope is \(0.999665 \times 0.000335 = 0.000335\), and \(0.25 / 0.000335 = 746\).

The tanh and the sigmoid

The tanh has the same problem in its tails, though its slope peaks at 1 instead of 0.25. In fact \(\tanh z = 2\sigma(2z) - 1\): it is the sigmoid stretched to run from \(-1\) to 1 and sharpened by a factor of 2 (0.3).

ReLU and GELU

ReLU has a slope of 1 for all positive \(z\), so it never saturates on that side. Its price is the other side: for negative \(z\) the slope is 0, and a neuron that sees only negative sums gets no signal at all. GELU is the smooth cousin. It multiplies \(z\) by \(\Phi(z)\), the chance that a standard normal value falls below \(z\) (0.7). Large positive \(z\) passes almost unchanged. Large negative \(z\) is squashed to almost 0. The corner at 0 is rounded. Hendrycks and Gimpel proposed it in 2016, and the original GPT and BERT language models use it (D5). The step has slope 0 wherever it is defined, so gradient descent has no slope to follow, and the perceptron of the next section uses its own rule.

How a ReLU unit dies

How does a ReLU unit die? Suppose its weights are \((0.5, 0.5)\) and one large update pushes its bias to \(-3\). The sum \(0.5 x_1 + 0.5 x_2 - 3\) is positive only when \(x_1 + x_2 > 6\). For two independent inputs, scaled to a spread of 1, the total \(x_1 + x_2\) has a spread of about 1.4. So 6 is more than four spreads out, and fewer than one input in 10,000 switches the unit on. With no input on there is no slope, no update and no way back. A variant called leaky ReLU keeps a small slope, such as 0.01, on the negative side, so that a unit cannot die completely.

The six activations in a table

activationoutput \(g(z)\)slope \(g'(z)\)output at \(z = 1\)slope at \(z = 1\)
none\(z\)\(1\)11
step\(1\) if \(z \ge 0\), otherwise \(0\)\(0\) (undefined at \(z = 0\))10
sigmoid\(\sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\)\(\sigma(z)\,\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr)\)0.7310.197
tanh\(\tanh z = \dfrac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{e^{z} + e^{-z}}\)\(1 - \tanh^{2} z\)0.7620.420
ReLU\(\max(0, z)\)\(1\) if \(z > 0\), otherwise \(0\)11
GELU\(z\,\Phi(z)\)\(\Phi(z) + z\,\varphi(z)\)0.8411.083
  • \(\Phi(z)\) is the cumulative normal curve: the share of a standard normal distribution below \(z\). \(\varphi(z)\) is the bell curve itself. Both come from 0.7.
  • The sigmoid slope \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\) is the rule from 0.6. At \(z = 0\) it is \(0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\).
  • At \(z = 0\) ReLU has a corner. Software picks a slope of 0 there, which almost never matters.
  • The last two columns are worked values. For GELU at \(z = 1\): \(\Phi(1) = 0.8413\) and \(\varphi(1) = 0.2420\), so the output is \(1 \times 0.8413 = 0.841\) and the slope is \(0.8413 + 1 \times 0.2420 = 1.083\). The slope is above 1 because the curve is still bending upwards there.

Steps behind the three slope rules

Show the steps behind the three slope rules

Sigmoid. Write \(\sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\). The chain rule (0.6) gives the slope of the outer power, then of the inner sum:

\[ \sigma'(z) = -(1 + e^{-z})^{-2}\cdot(-e^{-z}) = \frac{e^{-z}}{(1 + e^{-z})^{2}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\cdot\frac{e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}} = \sigma(z)\,\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr) \]

The last step uses \(1 - \sigma(z) = \dfrac{1 + e^{-z} - 1}{1 + e^{-z}} = \dfrac{e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}}\).

tanh. With \(u = e^{z} - e^{-z}\) and \(v = e^{z} + e^{-z}\) the slopes are \(u' = v\) and \(v' = u\). The quotient rule gives:

\[ \frac{d}{dz}\frac{u}{v} = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}} = \frac{v^{2} - u^{2}}{v^{2}} = 1 - \tanh^{2} z \]

GELU. It is a product \(z \cdot \Phi(z)\), so the product rule gives \(1\cdot\Phi(z) + z\,\Phi'(z)\), and the slope of the cumulative curve \(\Phi\) is the bell curve \(\varphi\).

In practice

In practice: ReLU is a common default for hidden layers, and GELU is used in several well-known transformer models. A sigmoid suits the output when the answer is a probability. No activation suits an output that can take any value, such as a temperature change. A frequent mistake is a ReLU at the output of a model that must predict values that can be negative: it can never output them.

When the slope cancels: the update of a weight usually contains the slope of the activation as a factor, as in the squared-error push of A3. A sigmoid output with log loss is the exception, because there the slope cancels and the push is \(p - y\).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a ReLU network does not learn at all, count how many neurons have a negative \(z\) for the whole batch. A neuron that is dead for all inputs has a slope of 0, so no update reaches it. A smaller learning rate and a sensible start often stop units dying (B8).

In Python

import numpy as np
from math import erf, sqrt

z = np.array([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0])
acts = {
    "none":    z,
    "step":    (z >= 0).astype(float),
    "sigmoid": 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)),
    "tanh":    np.tanh(z),
    "ReLU":    np.maximum(0, z),
    "GELU":    np.array([v * 0.5 * (1 + erf(v / sqrt(2))) for v in z]),
}
print("z        ", z)
for name, a in acts.items():
    print(f"{name:9s}", np.round(a, 3))
z         [-2.  0.  2.]
none      [-2.  0.  2.]
step      [0. 1. 1.]
sigmoid   [0.119 0.5   0.881]
tanh      [-0.964  0.     0.964]
ReLU      [0. 0. 2.]
GELU      [-0.046  0.     1.954]

The table is the figure in numbers: at \(z = -2\) the tanh and sigmoid are near their lower ends, ReLU is 0, and GELU is a little below 0.

You can check the slope formulas of the table without calculus. Move \(z\) a tiny step up and a tiny step down, take the change in the output and divide by the size of the two steps. The result matches the formulas: 0.1966 and 0.4200 at \(z = 1\), and 0.105 and 0.071 at \(z = 2\) for the sigmoid and the tanh.

import numpy as np
from math import erf, sqrt

sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
gelu = lambda z: z * 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))
relu = lambda z: max(0.0, z)
acts = {"sigmoid": sigmoid, "tanh": np.tanh, "ReLU": relu, "GELU": gelu}

h = 1e-5  # slope = change in output for a tiny change in z
for z in (1.0, 2.0, 8.0):
    row = [f"{name} {(f(z + h) - f(z - h)) / (2 * h):.4f}" for name, f in acts.items()]
    print(f"z = {z:.0f}:  " + "  ".join(row))
ratio = 0.25 / (sigmoid(8) * (1 - sigmoid(8)))
print("sigmoid slope at 0 over slope at 8:", round(ratio))
print("GELU(-1) =", round(gelu(-1.0), 3))
z = 1:  sigmoid 0.1966  tanh 0.4200  ReLU 1.0000  GELU 1.0833
z = 2:  sigmoid 0.1050  tanh 0.0707  ReLU 1.0000  GELU 1.0852

Where this is used

Used in: the slopes in this section are the factors that backpropagation multiplies together (B4). Saturated and dead units explain why deep networks need care with their start and their normalisation (B6).

More questions

What is GELU at \(z = -1\), and how does it differ from ReLU there?

\(\Phi(-1) = 0.1587\), so GELU\((-1) = -1 \times 0.1587 = -0.159\). ReLU gives 0. GELU lets a small negative value through, and its slope there is slightly negative (\(-0.083\)).

Fit a neuron to the sharks

Guess first. The made-up table has 200 milk sharks and 72 grey bamboo sharks, with a known length and depth for all 272. Always answering "milk shark" is right 73.5% of the time. Can one neuron with two inputs get to 90%?

The same two-input neuron can be a line (no activation), a logistic regression (the sigmoid) or a perceptron (the step). Which one it is depends on its activation and on the rule that fits it. Fitting, also called training, adjusts the weights and the bias step by step with a rule that lowers an error measure. This usually raises the accuracy, the share of the 272 sharks called correctly. A call is the class that the output points to. A perceptron is a neuron with a step activation, and its rule changes the weights only when a call is wrong.

  1. Navy circles are milk sharks, coral diamonds are bamboo sharks, and a dark ring marks a wrong call. Choose the sigmoid and press "Train": the rule adjusts the weights and the bias, and the accuracy stops changing near 249 of 272 (91.5%).
  2. Choose "step", press "Reset the dials" and then "Train": over the first 40 steps (one step is one pass over the 272 sharks) the accuracy keeps changing between about 80% and 91%.

A sigmoid neuron reaches 91.5% (249 of 272) on the sharks it was fitted to, against 73.5% for the lazy answer; a step neuron's accuracy keeps changing.

How it works

The perceptron rule adds \(\eta\,(y - \hat{y})\) times the shark's input to the weights and \(\eta\,(y - \hat{y})\) to the bias. Here \(y\) is the label (1 for bamboo, 0 for milk), \(\hat{y}\) is the call and \(\eta\) is the learning rate, the size of one step. Take Tag 4127, a bamboo shark (\(y = 1\)) with scaled length \(-1.45\) and scaled depth \(-1.87\) (scaled over the 272 sharks). A step neuron with weights 0 and 0 and bias \(-0.1\) has \(z = -0.1\), so its call is "milk" (\(\hat{y} = 0\)) and \(y - \hat{y} = 1\). With \(\eta = 0.1\) the rule changes the weights by \(0.1 \times 1 \times (-1.45) = -0.145\) and \(0.1 \times 1 \times (-1.87) = -0.187\), and the bias by \(+0.1\). The new \(z\) is \((-0.145) \times (-1.45) + (-0.187) \times (-1.87) + 0 = 0.56\), so the call flips to "bamboo".

\(w_1\)new weight, −0.145=\(w_1\)old weight, 0+\(\eta\)learning rate, 0.1×\(y-\hat{y}\)label minus call, 1×\(x_1\)scaled length, −1.45

On a wrong call the rule moves the weights towards the shark's input when \(y - \hat{y} = 1\), which raises \(z\), and away from it when \(y - \hat{y} = -1\), which lowers \(z\).

Common belief. Train a perceptron for long enough and it reaches the best line and stays there.

Why it fails. When the classes overlap, as here, some shark is always wrong, so the rule never stops changing the weights.

Better account. The sigmoid neuron outputs \(p = \sigma(z)\), read as the probability of "bamboo", and log loss is large when \(p\) is far from the label \(y\). Averaged over the sharks, the updates \(\eta\,(y - p)\) times the input cancel at the lowest point of log loss. So training stops changing the weights there, even when the classes overlap.

Quick quiz

A perceptron calls a juvenile shark "adult" (label 0, call 1). Which way does the update move the weights?

\(y - \hat{y} = -1\), so the weights move by \(-\eta\) times the shark's input: away from it. That lowers the shark's \(z\), which pushes the call towards 0.

Why does training reach one setting for the sigmoid neuron but not for the perceptron, when the classes overlap?

For the sigmoid neuron the updates cancel on average at the lowest point of log loss, so the average update is 0 there. The perceptron changes the weights by a full step whenever any shark is called wrong, so it keeps changing them while some sharks stay wrong.

Go deeper sigmoid update, trained dials, Python about 10 min

Reading the figure

The star is Tag 4127, the juvenile bamboo shark from the Juhu rock pool (44.0 cm, found at 0.4 m). First tune the dials by hand, then press "Train" and see what the training rule does with the sigmoid. Switch to "none", "tanh" and "step" and train again from "Reset the dials". The inputs are scaled as in A2, so the weights are comparable: negative weights on length and depth mean that shorter, shallower sharks are more likely bamboo.

Three activations, three old friends

With no activation the neuron computes \(\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b\). Fitting minimises squared error, so this is linear regression (A2), here fitted to the labels 0 and 1, and it reaches 90.1%. With a sigmoid it computes a probability and training minimises log loss, which for one shark is \(-\ln p\) if the label is 1 and \(-\ln(1 - p)\) if the label is 0, averaged over the sharks: this is logistic regression (A3), the update is the same loop of A3, and it reaches 91.5%. With tanh the accuracy is 91.2%. With a step it calls "bamboo" when \(z \ge 0\), and it is the perceptron, one of the first neural networks. It cannot use the slope, which is 0. Rosenblatt's perceptron rule moves the weights directly. For a shark with label \(y\) and call \(\hat{y}\), the update adds \(\eta\,(y - \hat{y})\) times the input.

Why the call flips

The update adds \(\eta\,(y - \hat{y})\) times the shark's own input vector to the weights, so the weighted sum \(z\) of that shark changes by \(\eta\,(y - \hat{y})\,(x_1^2 + x_2^2 + 1)\), where the last 1 comes from the bias. The scaled inputs of Tag 4127 come from the mean and spread of the 272 sharks: \((44.0 - 61.571)/12.151 = -1.446\) for length and \((0.4 - 25.191)/13.246 = -1.872\) for depth. Then \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 + 1 = 2.09 + 3.50 + 1 = 6.59\), and \(z\) rises by \(0.1 \times 1 \times 6.59 = 0.66\), from \(-0.10\) to \(+0.56\), as the working in the text above also shows. The new weights make \(z\) larger, which is the direction that can fix the call, and the call flips to "bamboo". A small step can fix one shark and break another, which is why the rule needs several passes.

The same step for the sigmoid

0.177new \(w_1\)=0.50old \(w_1\)−0.5learning rate \(\eta\)×−0.447\(p - y = 0.553 - 1\)×−1.45scaled length

The sigmoid neuron makes the same kind of move with a soft size. At the starting dials of the figure (\(\mathbf{w} = (0.5, -0.5)\), \(b = 0\)) the weighted sum of Tag 4127 is \(z = 0.21\) and the output is \(p = 0.553\). The gap to the label is \(p - y = -0.447\), the push of A3. For this shark alone, \(w_1\) moves from 0.50 to \(0.5 - 0.5 \times (-0.447) \times (-1.45) = 0.177\) and \(w_2\) from \(-0.50\) to \(-0.918\). For this shark the step shrinks as \(p\) gets closer to the label 1, while the perceptron takes a full step whenever the call is wrong. The figure averages these steps over all 272 sharks.

Symbols

\[ \hat{y} = \begin{cases} 1 & z \ge 0\\ 0 & z < 0 \end{cases} \qquad w_j \leftarrow w_j + \eta\,(y - \hat{y})\,x_j \qquad b \leftarrow b + \eta\,(y - \hat{y}) \]

  • \(y\) is the true label (1 for bamboo, 0 for milk) and \(\hat{y}\) is the call. When they agree, \(y - \hat{y} = 0\) and the weights stay put.
  • \(x_j\) is input \(j\) after scaling. A wrong call on a shark adds a multiple of that shark's input vector to the weights for a bamboo shark called milk, and subtracts it for a milk shark called bamboo, so the dashed line turns to move that shark towards the other side.
  • For the sigmoid the update of A3 has the same form, with the soft difference \(y - p\) in place of \(y - \hat{y}\).

Where the dials end up for the sigmoid

Where do the dials end up for the sigmoid? Training the neuron on all 272 sharks gives a weight of \(-2.84\) on length, a weight of \(-0.92\) on depth, and a bias of \(-2.06\). Both weights are negative, so short, shallow sharks look like bamboo sharks, and per spread of the input the weight on length is about three times the weight on depth. Try Tag 1224, a milk shark of 67.8 cm found at 39.4 m. Its scaled inputs are 0.513 and 1.073:

0.011chance of bamboo=σ(−2.84weight on length×0.513scaled length+−0.92weight on depth×1.073scaled depth+−2.06bias)

The sum is \(-1.46 - 0.99 - 2.06 = -4.50\), and \(\sigma(-4.50) = 0.011\). The output 0.011 means a 1.1% chance of bamboo, so the call is "milk", with a 99% chance, and that is right. For Tag 4127 the scaled inputs \((-1.45, -1.87)\) give \(z = 4.11 + 1.73 - 2.06 = 3.78\) and a bamboo chance of 0.978. The call is right again.

What the headline accuracy hides

The headline accuracy hides a difference. Of the 200 milk sharks the neuron calls 194 right. Of the 72 bamboo sharks it calls only 55 right, about 76%. Of its 23 mistakes, 17 are bamboo sharks called milk. The neuron beats the lazy answer "milk", yet it misses one bamboo shark in four (A4). The accuracy of 91.5% is measured on the 272 sharks that were used to fit the dials. Fitting on four fifths of the sharks and measuring on the other fifth, five times over, gives 247 right, or 90.8%, an accuracy on sharks that were not used for fitting. That is a little below 91.5% (A4). The code below reads catch.csv of the shark data and does all of this.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

d = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")
d = d[d.species.isin(["milk", "bamboo"])]  # 200 milk, 72 bamboo (made up)
X = d[["length_cm", "depth_m"]].to_numpy()
y = (d.species == "bamboo").to_numpy().astype(float)

def fit(X, y, steps=20000, eta=0.5):
    mean, spread = X.mean(axis=0), X.std(axis=0)
    Z = (X - mean) / spread  # scale both inputs
    w, b = np.zeros(2), 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):  # log loss gradient descent, as in A3
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(Z @ w + b)))
        w -= eta * Z.T @ (p - y) / len(y)
        b -= eta * np.mean(p - y)
    return w, b, mean, spread

w, b, mean, spread = fit(X, y)
call = ((X - mean) / spread) @ w + b > 0
print("weights", w.round(2), "bias", round(b, 2))
print("right:", (call == y).sum(), "of", len(y))
print("milk right:", (~call & (y == 0)).sum(), "of", int((y == 0).sum()),
      "  bamboo right:", (call & (y == 1)).sum(), "of", int(y.sum()))
for tag in (4127, 1224):
    r = d[d.record_id == tag].iloc[0]
    z = w @ ((np.array([r.length_cm, r.depth_m]) - mean) / spread) + b
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
    print(f"Tag {tag} ({r.species}): z = {z:.2f}, chance of bamboo = {p:.3f}")

order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(y))
folds = np.array_split(order, 5)  # fit on 4/5, score on 1/5
right = 0
for test in folds:
    train = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), test)
    wf, bf, mf, sf = fit(X[train], y[train])
    right += ((((X[test] - mf) / sf) @ wf + bf > 0) == y[test]).sum()
print("5-fold score:", right, "of", len(y), f"= {right / len(y):.3f}")
weights [-2.84 -0.92] bias -2.06
right: 249 of 272
milk right: 194 of 200   bamboo right: 55 of 72
Tag 4127 (bamboo): z = 3.78, chance of bamboo = 0.978
Tag 1224 (milk): z = -4.50, chance of bamboo = 0.011
5-fold score: 247 of 272 = 0.908

The perceptron on eight sharks

When one line can separate the classes with no mistakes, the perceptron rule is guaranteed to stop. When no such line exists, it cannot stop. The perceptron takes a full step for any wrong call, while the sigmoid neuron takes a soft step.

import numpy as np

# 8 made-up sharks: length (cm), depth (m), label 1 = bamboo, 0 = milk
X = np.array([[58, 14], [49, 20], [66, 30], [54, 6], [70, 24], [46, 12], [62, 18], [57, 3]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1])
X = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)        # scale both inputs

w, b, eta = np.zeros(2), 0.0, 0.1
for epoch in range(1, 21):
    mistakes = 0
    for x, label in zip(X, y):
        call = 1 if w @ x + b >= 0 else 0       # step activation
        if call != label:
            w += eta * (label - call) * x       # move towards the right class
            b += eta * (label - call)
            mistakes += 1
    print(f"epoch {epoch}: {mistakes} mistakes, w = {np.round(w, 3)}, b = {b:.2f}")
    if mistakes == 0:
        break
epoch 1: 3 mistakes, w = [-0.167 -0.046], b = 0.10
epoch 2: 1 mistakes, w = [-0.17  -0.024], b = 0.00
epoch 3: 0 mistakes, w = [-0.17  -0.024], b = 0.00

With eight sharks that one line can separate, the rule stops after three passes. With the 272 sharks of the figure it never stops, as the break box above says.

Here is the first pass of that printout, step by step. All the dials start at 0, so shark 1 (58 cm, 14 m, scaled to \((0.033, -0.222)\)) has \(z = 0\). A step neuron calls \(z \ge 0\) a 1, and the label is 0, so the call is wrong. Sharks 2 and 4 are wrong in turn. The other five are called right and leave the dials as they are.

sharkweighted sum \(z\)calllabel\(\mathbf{w}\) after\(b\) after
10.00010(\(-0.003\), 0.022)\(-0.10\)
2\(-0.085\)01(\(-0.118\), 0.071)0.00
4\(-0.025\)01(\(-0.167\), \(-0.046\))0.10

Take shark 2 (49 cm, 20 m, scaled to \((-1.147, 0.489)\)). Its weighted sum is \(-0.003 \times (-1.147) + 0.022 \times 0.489 - 0.10 = -0.085\), so the call is 0 while the label is 1. The update adds \(0.1 \times 1\) times the shark's inputs: \(w_1 = -0.003 + 0.1 \times (-1.147) = -0.118\) and \(w_2 = 0.022 + 0.1 \times 0.489 = 0.071\). The bias goes from \(-0.10\) to 0. A fix for one shark can break another, so a second pass checks them all again.

In practice

In practice: with inputs scaled to a spread of 1, learning rates between 0.01 and 1 are typical for a single neuron. A smooth activation with a smooth loss is the usual remedy for overlapping classes. If all the dials start at 0, the learning rate of the perceptron only rescales the weights and never changes a call. The perceptron rule is rarely used for training today. It is taught because it shows learning as small corrections. Logistic regression replaced the perceptron rule in most work, because the sigmoid with log loss settles on one answer even when the classes overlap.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Compare the accuracy with the lazy answer before you accept it: here 73.5%. If the accuracy stays at that number and the dials do not move, look for a dead start. With ReLU, press "Random start" a few times: from some starts \(z\) is negative for all sharks, the slope is 0 and the dials stay put.

Where this is used

Used in: the perceptron rule is one of the oldest learning rules for a neuron (Rosenblatt, 1958). Its failure on XOR is a main reason for hidden layers (B2). The log-loss update behind the sigmoid neuron is the one that B4 sends back through a whole network.

More questions

For Tag 4127 the trained neuron gives \(p = 0.978\) and the label is 1. What is \(p - y\), and how does it compare with the \(-0.447\) at the starting dials?

\(p - y = 0.978 - 1 = -0.022\), about 20 times smaller than \(-0.447\). The neuron is nearly right about this shark, so the update from this shark moves the dials very little.

A layer is many neurons

Guess first. Three neurons read the same two inputs, with separate weights and separate biases. How many numbers does the layer have in all, and can you write the three weighted sums as one matrix product?

A layer is a set of \(n\) neurons that read the same \(d\) inputs side by side, and \(n\) is its width. A vector is a list of numbers: the inputs form the vector \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(d\) entries, and the biases form the vector \(\mathbf{b}\) with \(n\) entries. The weights form the weight matrix \(W\), a table with one row per neuron and one column per input, so \(n \times d\) numbers. The layer computes all \(n\) weighted sums as one matrix product, and its output vector \(\mathbf{a}\) lists the \(n\) outputs.

  1. Type new numbers into the table of weights and biases, or move the sliders for \(x_1\) and \(x_2\): the boxes under the table redo the computation as a matrix product.
  2. The three small maps show the outputs of neurons 1, 2 and 3 over the plane of the inputs. Their stripes point in different directions because the weights differ.
  3. Choose "ReLU" and look for a neuron whose output is 0: its map is flat on the side where \(z\) is negative.

The first row of the table is the neuron of section 1 (\(z = 1.10\), \(a = 0.750\)), and the three rows together are one matrix product.

How it works

For \(x_1 = 0.8\) and \(x_2 = 0.4\) the three neurons give \(z = 1.10\), \(0.30\) and \(-0.60\), from \(1.5 \times 0.8 - 1.0 \times 0.4 + 0.3\), \(0.5 \times 0.8 + 1.0 \times 0.4 - 0.5\) and \(-1.0 \times 0.8 + 0.5 \times 0.4 + 0\). With the sigmoid the outputs are 0.750, 0.574 and 0.354.

The matrix \(W\) is 3 × 2 here: row \(i\) contains the weights of neuron \(i\), and \(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\) gives all \(n\) weighted sums together. The layer has \(n \times d\) weights and \(n\) biases, which is \(n\,(d + 1)\) numbers: \(3 \times 3 = 9\) here, the answer to the guess.

Common belief. The neurons in a layer exchange information with one another.

Why it fails. The activation \(g\) is applied to the entries of \(\mathbf{z}\) separately, and an entry depends only on its own row of \(W\) and its own bias.

Better account. The neurons in a layer differ only in their weights and biases. Two neurons with the same weights and bias give the same output for any input. If the weights that use their outputs are also equal, they receive the same updates and stay copies of one another. This is why training starts from different random weights (deep networks).

Quick quiz

A layer has 4 neurons and 6 inputs. What are the dimensions of \(W\), and how many numbers does the layer have?

\(W\) has 4 rows and 6 columns. The layer has \(4 \times 6 + 4 = 28\) numbers: 24 weights and 4 biases.

Two neurons in a layer have identical weights and biases. What does the layer gain from the second one?

It gains no new information. Both give the same output for all inputs, so the second adds a copy of the first.

Reading the figure

Type new numbers into the table, or move the two input sliders. The three small maps show the neurons one by one: the output over the plane of the inputs, with the teal dot at the current input. A map shows the stripes of a single neuron, and the stripes point in different directions because the weights differ. The bracketed boxes below the table show the same computation as a matrix product, the form that code and graphics cards use. Choose "ReLU" and look for a neuron whose output is 0: its map is flat on the side where \(z\) is negative.

More examples of counting

The softmax classifier of A3 is a layer with \(n = 5\), one neuron per species, followed by softmax: \(5 \times 3 = 15\) numbers. A layer of 8 neurons that reads 6 shark measurements has \(8 \times 6 + 8 = 56\) numbers.

The same layer with ReLU

With ReLU the outputs for \(\mathbf{x} = (0.8, 0.4)\) are 1.10, 0.30 and 0: neuron 3 is switched off for this input, but it may be on for another.

Two inputs at once

Now give the layer two inputs at once, \(\mathbf{x}_1 = (0.8, 0.4)\) and \(\mathbf{x}_2 = (-0.5, 0.9)\), as the two rows of a matrix \(X\). The product \(XW^\top + \mathbf{b}\) has one row of three sums per input. Here \(W^\top\) is \(W\) with its rows and columns swapped.

\[ \begin{aligned} XW^\top + \mathbf{b} &= \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.4 \\ -0.5 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 0.5 & -1.0 \\ -1.0 & 1.0 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0.3 & -0.5 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} 1.10 & 0.30 & -0.60 \\ -1.35 & 0.15 & 0.95 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} \]

The first row is the case above. For the second input the first neuron gives \(1.5 \times (-0.5) - 1.0 \times 0.9 + 0.3 = -1.35\). The second gives \(0.5 \times (-0.5) + 1.0 \times 0.9 - 0.5 = 0.15\). The third gives \(-1.0 \times (-0.5) + 0.5 \times 0.9 + 0 = 0.95\). With ReLU this input switches neuron 1 off and neuron 3 on, the opposite of the first input. With the sigmoid the outputs are 0.206, 0.537 and 0.721. Which neurons are on depends on where the input lies, so a layer describes different inputs in different ways.

Layers with many inputs

The count grows fast with the number of inputs, and that limits this kind of layer. A layer of 100 neurons that reads a small 64 by 64 grey photo has 4,096 inputs and \(100 \times 4096 + 100 = 409{,}700\) numbers. A weight belongs to one pixel position, so a shark shifted by ten pixels is a new input to the layer. Photo models use a layer that shares weights across positions (C1).

Symbols

\[ \mathbf{z} = W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b} \qquad \mathbf{a} = g(\mathbf{z}) \qquad \text{number of parameters} = n\,(d + 1) \]

  • \(W\) has \(n\) rows and \(d\) columns: one row per neuron and one column per input. \(\mathbf{x}\) has \(d\) entries, and \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{z}\) have \(n\) entries.
  • \(g\) is applied to the entries of \(\mathbf{z}\) separately, so the neurons in a layer do not talk to one another.
  • Layers are written with a number in square brackets, \(W^{[1]}\) for the first, when a network has several (B2).

A comparison: a panel of experts

A layer is like a panel of experts who look at the same photo and report one number apiece. The comparison fits because the neurons read the same inputs. It breaks where the break box in the text above says: the experts never hear one another, and their only difference is their weights.

In practice

In practice: layers are rarely as narrow as three. Widths from a few dozen to a few thousand are common, because a graphics card multiplies one large matrix faster than many small ones. Inputs go in as a batch of sharks, one row per shark, so the product becomes \(X W^\top + \mathbf{b}\) (0.5). A layer's outputs mean little one at a time. They are useful as a group, which the next chapter builds on.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Print the dimensions of the arrays before you multiply, as in the first line of the code below. For \(n\) neurons and \(d\) inputs they should be \((n, d)\), \((d,)\) and \((n,)\). Swapping the rows and columns of \(W\) gives an error, or, worse, a plausible but wrong answer when \(n = d\).

In Python

import numpy as np

W = np.array([[1.5, -1.0], [0.5, 1.0], [-1.0, 0.5]])   # 3 neurons, 2 inputs: one row per neuron
b = np.array([0.3, -0.5, 0.0])
x = np.array([0.8, 0.4])
print(W.shape, x.shape, b.shape)                        # expect (3, 2) (2,) (3,)

z = W @ x + b                                           # three weighted sums at once
a = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))                                # sigmoid on all three
print("z =", np.round(z, 2))
print("a =", np.round(a, 3))
print("numbers in the layer:", W.size + b.size)
(3, 2) (2,) (3,)
z = [ 1.1  0.3 -0.6]
a = [0.75  0.574 0.354]
numbers in the layer: 9

The same layer on a batch is one line of code. Row \(i\) of the result has the three sums for input \(i\). In \(X\) and in the result, the first dimension counts inputs.

import numpy as np

W = np.array([[1.5, -1.0], [0.5, 1.0], [-1.0, 0.5]])  # the layer of section 4
b = np.array([0.3, -0.5, 0.0])
X = np.array([[0.8, 0.4], [-0.5, 0.9]])  # two inputs, one per row

Z = X @ W.T + b  # all sums for both inputs at once
print("X", X.shape, "W.T", W.T.shape, "Z", Z.shape)
print("z =\n", Z)
print("sigmoid =\n", np.round(1 / (1 + np.exp(-Z)), 3))
print("ReLU =\n", np.maximum(0, Z))

Where this is used

Used in: a network is a stack of such layers, and B2 shows why a stack needs an activation between its layers. The five outputs of the species classifier in A3 are a layer of five neurons.

A neural network is built from one small part, used many times: the neuron.

More questions

A layer of 8 neurons reads a 64 by 64 grey photo, flattened to 4,096 inputs. How many numbers does it have?

\(8 \times 4096 + 8 = 32{,}776\): 32,768 weights and 8 biases.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A sigmoid neuron has \(w_1 = 2\), \(w_2 = -1\) and \(b = -1\). Compute \(z\) and the output for \(\mathbf{x} = (1, 3)\) and for \(\mathbf{x} = (3, 1)\). Write the line \(z = 0\) as \(x_2 = \dots\).

    Hint

    Use \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) and solve \(2x_1 - x_2 - 1 = 0\) for \(x_2\).

  2. theory Show that \(\tanh z = 2\sigma(2z) - 1\). What does this say about a tanh neuron with weights \(\mathbf{w}\) and bias \(b\), compared with a sigmoid neuron with weights \(2\mathbf{w}\) and bias \(2b\)? Where is the line \(z = 0\) in the two cases?

    Hint

    Write \(\sigma(2z) = 1/(1 + e^{-2z})\), multiply the top and bottom of \(2\sigma(2z) - 1\) by \(e^{z}\), and compare with the definition of tanh.

  3. theory A perceptron has \(\mathbf{w} = (0.2, -0.1)\), \(b = 0\) and \(\eta = 0.5\). A shark with scaled inputs \((1.0, 2.0)\) has label 0. Find the call, then apply one update, then check the new call.

  4. theory A layer has 5 neurons and 6 inputs. How many weights and biases does it have? A second layer has 3 neurons that read the 5 outputs of the first. How many numbers does the second layer have?

Practice

  1. practice Take the neuron of section 1: \(\mathbf{w} = (4.732, -0.1215)\), \(b = 2.4811\), inputs scaled with mean \((39.138, 10.993)\) and spread \((8.614, 2.455)\). Compute its output for Tag 4127 (44.0 cm, girth 12.4 cm) and Tag 5519 (82.0 cm, girth 27.6 cm). Compare with the table of A3.

  2. practice Load catch.csv with pandas, keep the milk and bamboo sharks, scale length and depth, and train the perceptron of section 3 in the order of the table. Print the score after 1, 10 and 100 passes. Then fit a sigmoid neuron with the loop of A3 and compare.

  3. practice Stack the scaled inputs of Tags 3305, 4127 and 5519 into an array \(X\) with three rows. Compute the weighted sums of the three neurons of section 4 for all three sharks at once with X @ W.T + b, then apply the sigmoid for the outputs. Print the dimensions of all the arrays and say which dimension counts sharks.

Think deeper

  1. open The perceptron and the sigmoid neuron both draw one line through the milk and bamboo sharks. Design a test that tells you which line you should trust for new sharks. What data would you keep aside, and what would you compare?

  2. open SharkCam needs three single-neuron outputs. (a) The weight of a shark in kg. (b) Whether the frame has a shark in it. (c) The change in water temperature since the last dive, which can be negative. Choose an activation for all three and explain what goes wrong with the others.

  3. open A friend says: "A step neuron is the most natural, because the answer is yes or no." Give two reasons why modern networks use activations with a slope (ReLU, GELU, sigmoid) instead of a step, and say when a step output is still the right thing to show the user.

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week, before you open the answers.

A neuron has no activation, one input and squared error. Which model from Part A is it, and what is its update rule for the slope?

It is the line of A2. With residuals \(r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\), the update is \(w \leftarrow w + \eta\,\tfrac{2}{m}\sum_i r_i x_i\).

A sigmoid neuron gives a juvenile shark (label 0) the probability 0.9 of being an adult. Compare the push on the weighted sum \(z\) from log loss with the push from squared error (A3).

Log loss pushes with \(p - y = 0.9\). Squared error pushes with \(2(p - y)\,p\,(1 - p) = 2 \times 0.9 \times 0.9 \times 0.1 = 0.162\), about 5.6 times smaller, because the sigmoid is flat there.

One straight line cannot separate XOR (0.4). What does that say about a single neuron with an activation that never decreases (all but GELU), and what would you add to fix it?

A single neuron's decision has one straight boundary line, so it cannot do XOR. More neurons, arranged in layers with a bend between them, can. That is B2.

Sources and further reading

  1. Rosenblatt, F. (1958). The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. Psychological Review, 65(6), 386–408. doi:10.1037/h0042519. The perceptron and its learning rule.
  2. Hendrycks, D. and Gimpel, K. (2016). Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs). arXiv:1606.08415. arxiv.org/abs/1606.08415. The definition \(z\,\Phi(z)\).
  3. Radford, A., Narasimhan, K., Salimans, T. and Sutskever, I. (2018). Improving language understanding by generative pre-training. OpenAI. PDF. The original GPT uses GELU. Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K. and Toutanova, K. (2019). BERT: pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers for language understanding. NAACL-HLT 2019, 4171–4186. arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805. BERT uses GELU too.
  4. CS231n: Deep Learning for Computer Vision, Stanford. Neural Networks Part 1: setting up the architecture, on sigmoid, tanh and ReLU. cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-1. Saturation of the sigmoid and dying ReLU units.
  5. Sanderson, G. (3Blue1Brown). But what is a neural network? lesson page. Neurons, weights and biases drawn step by step.
  6. Smilkov, D. and Carter, S. A Neural Network Playground (TensorFlow Playground). playground.tensorflow.org. The model for letting readers change a network and watch the output map.
